Discussion We sought to describe the spatiotemporal distribution and co-occurrence of cryptic Culex species across an urbanization gradient using molecular identification and community modeling approaches. Although these cryptic Culex species are sympatric, we found that most collections comprised 1–2 Culex species and collections containing all three species were uncommon. When all three did occur together, they were limited to suburban areas or urban areas early in the season. Culex pipiens is commonly considered the primary bridge vector of WNv to humans due to high vector competence, high infection rate in the field and the laboratory, high abundance, and willingness to feed on both birds and mammals ( , ). Culex pipiens dominated our collections across sites and were not closely associated with any season, site class, or landscape feature, demonstrating their generalist habitat preferences and expansive distribution. This poses challenges for vector control organizations, whose available management resources likely reach only a fraction of the broader Cx. pipiens population. For example, State of Maryland vector control begins larvicide application in March to suppress early season population growth. Yet, most labor and financial resources must be reserved to address localized nuisance complaints in the late spring or summer, or for regional mosquito suppression in areas where pathogen-positive mosquito pools (inclusive of WNv) are collected (Brian Prendergast, personal communication). Targeted early spring management would likely make the greatest impact on Cx. pipiens population growth and human WNv transmission, but locating ovipositional sites and refugia remains difficult. Further research on the life history and ecology of Cx. pipiens may facilitate identification of ovipositional habitats and overwintering refugia, and provide vector control operators with additional creative, targeted strategies for WNv management. Site class and environmental features were important in determining which cryptic Culex species co-occurred with Cx. pipiens at each site. Collections in rural and suburban environments often contained Cx. pipiens and Cx. restuans, while Cx. pipiens and Cx. quinquefasciatus were primarily collected together in urban environments. Culex quinquefasciatus were found at low but consistent levels across the season. We identified Cx. quinquefasciatus across site classes but most commonly in urban environments, commercial environments and at non-urban sites closest to the city center, suggesting they may disperse from a primary population in the city center. There was some evidence of hybridization between Cx . quinquefasciatus and Cx. pipiens . We speculate that there is limited gene flow between these taxa in our region based on our HWE analysis, despite their seasonal and spatial overlap in distribution. Interestingly, Cx. quinquefasciatus relative abundance was highest early and late in the season. This may be due to their inability to diapause, which likely results in their environmental persistence until seasonal conditions become unsuitable, leading to mortality or requiring them to seek refuge. High percent impervious surface, urban heat, and dense subterranean networks are hallmarks of commercial city centers, as are small containers in which Cx. quinquefasciatus are likely to oviposit ( ). We propose that a combination of the urban heat island effect and insulated, linked subterranean habitat in commercial areas support this species better than urban residential areas due to overwintering thermal limitations ( , ). We demonstrated that Cx. restuans were associated with rural, natural, and agricultural sites with low impervious surface furthest from the city center. They were rarely collected in urban environments, suggesting they may use these environments but are either ill-suited to them, or outcompeted by congeners that are highly adapted to anthropogenic environmental features, such as Cx. pipiens and Cx. quinquefasciatus . For instance, the fewest Cx. restuans (n=7) and most Cx. quinquefasciatus (n=27) were identified from the belowground site, which demonstrated the most pronounced anthropogenic and urban characteristics (see ). Normalized Differential Vegetation Index (NDVI) was high across rural sites ( ) yet was not independently found to be an important factor for species assemblages in any ordination ( ). Natural and agricultural sites had high total vegetation but hosted different Culex species assemblages, suggesting that composition of vegetation types influences species distributions. Cx. restuans were found at rural natural sites more often than they were at rural agricultural sites. This was consistent with previous work suggesting that the most important characteristics of Cx. restuans habitat included presence of evergreen forests and herbaceous vegetation, as well as high humidity ( ). Conversely, rural Cx. quinquefasciatus collections tended to be at agricultural sites closest to the city, with high overall vegetation but not necessarily a diverse canopy. We speculate that plants in monoculture, such as those found in agroecosystems, do not offer the same resources for mosquitoes as the diverse vegetation and heterogeneous canopy available in forests. We speculate that plants in monoculture, such as those found in agroecosystems, do not offer the same resources for mosquitoes as the diverse vegetation and heterogeneous canopy available in forests. For example, Culex restuans may not thrive in agricultural fields with no overstory, and the consequent high heat and low humidity. Culex quinquefasciatus exploit human-generated water sources common at both urban and agricultural sites for resting and oviposition, and therefore may rely less on natural environmental humidity and water sources ( , ). Moreover, Culex restuans were the only truly native species in our study and were prevalent in natural environments. Natural sites are least disturbed and may be most resistant to establishment of species undergoing range expansion and establishment, like Cx. quinquefasciatus and, to a lesser extent, Cx. pipiens . Use of natural, forested areas by Cx. restuans may enhance their role in WNV transmission in the early season at higher latitudes due to wet conditions in natural areas after snowmelt or in regions with high spring rainfall. Our findings support Cx. restuans as an early season species in greater Washington, D.C., which emerges prior to the start of the local mosquito management season. Yet assemblages do not change with season when local management occurs, in the months of June-October. The importance of early season Cx. restuans populations to WNv transmission is uncertain. In the eastern USA, human WNv cases generally appear in August and September (week of the year (WOY) 30–35), and infected mosquitoes are rarely collected before late July (WOY 28; , ). In a survey of Culex vectors in Connecticut, Cx. restuans were abundant much earlier in the season than Cx. pipiens , but WNv positive Cx. restuans were not collected until mid-July ( ). In Virginia, a single WNv positive Cx. restuans pool was identified in early May, but WNv was not commonly identified in Cx. restuans until late June ( ). We observed a high abundance of Cx. restuans in rural environments early in the collection season, and consequently at the very beginning of vector surveillance and abatement in our region. Surveillance may not capture mosquitoes at sites where early season amplification occurs, like natural areas. Low risk of human cases in these areas likely means that vector control resources are focused elsewhere. Studies speculate that a community of co-occurring Culex species may increase and extend WNv transmission across time and space due to differences in phenology, habitat use, and host preferences ( ). Our work documented a spring shift in Culex community composition in metropolitan Washington D.C. From June to October, however, when WNv is detected in mosquitoes and human cases occur, environmental features, and especially characteristics representative of urbanization, are the primary predictors of the Culex community assemblage across the landscape. The patterns of seasonality, habitat use, and abundance we observed may inform where and when populations of cryptic Culex are likely to contribute most to disease transmission. Culex restuans emerged first, and are most common in natural, forested sites. These types of sites are not currently prioritized for management due to low human population density, but interventions aimed at suppressing early spring populations should reduce WNv amplification throughout the season, and ultimately human cases. This may be challenging with our current tools, which partially rely on broad spectrum insecticides and can impact non-target invertebrate species. Further research that prioritizes understanding Culex overwintering behavior and refugia, especially for Cx. restuans, could improve targeted management of the first generation of this species each spring. Culex quinquefasciatus were limited to urban areas, perhaps due to their need for refugia from overwintering thermal limitations (Samy et al. 2016). Outside of those optimal conditions the contributions of Cx . quinquefasciatus in Washington D.C. and Maryland are likely to be comparatively low. However, viral amplification among non-diapausing Cx. quinquefasciatus that feed on avian and human hosts could be responsible for early season WNv initiation and late season spillover to humans. Culex pipiens were cosmopolitan and dominant across the landscape, especially after the spring seasonal shift, and are likely responsible for much of the WNv transmission, amplification, and epizootic spillover in our region. Studies exploring patterns of WNv-positive mosquito pools are common in the literature, such as those reviewed in Rochlin et al. (2019), but uncertainty about the distributions of cryptic Culex contributing to positive mosquito pools on fine scales remains. Future studies analyzing the spatiotemporal dynamics of community structure in other US metropolitan areas may elucidate the role of both landscape and phenology in assemblage dynamics and establish whether the patterns we observed are universal. Introduction The Nairoviridae family represents a group of tick-borne arboviruses expected to expand in their distribution with the effect of global warming. These viruses display a structure made of a negative-sense single-stranded tri-segmented RNA genome encapsulated in a lipid-based envelope ( ). Of this family, recently classified into the Hareavirales order of the class Bunyaviricetes ( ), the Orthonairovirus genus contains fifteen distinct viral species ( ), two of which are of most concern for human and animal health: Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) and Nairobi sheep disease virus (NSDV). CCHFV is the most notable orthonairovirus, able to cause Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) in humans. Fever, nausea and myalgia occur in the early-stage of human CCHF infections, before the disease progresses with haemorrhagic symptoms (petechiae, hematomas), resulting in a mortality rate of 3-30% ( ). Birds, ruminants and other small mammals have been shown to support CCHFV infections without the onset of symptoms, facilitating a tick-vertebrate-tick life cycle through which CCHFV circulates ( ). CCHFV has a reported widespread distribution in small ruminant populations across Eastern Europe, Southern Asia and the African continent, following the distribution of its principal vectors, the Hyalomma species of ticks ( ), and more recently, Rhipicephalus species ( ). The second orthonairovirus of concern, NSDV, is the aetiological agent of Nairobi sheep disease (NSD). Several stages characterize an NSD infection, where small ruminants display fever, lethargy and depressive behavior before severe haemorrhagic gastroenteritis ensues ( ). While small ruminants in enzootic regions are often protected by maternal antibodies, NSD is highly lethal in naïve individuals, with mortality rates that can reach 90% as previously recorded within populations imported into enzootic areas ( , ). Historical evidence suggests that symptomatic NSDV infections in humans are extremely rare, with exposed laboratory personnel working on NSDV in the 1970s being one of the few previously reported cases, where NSDV was determined as the cause of a febrile illness ( ). NSDV has an understudied tick-vertebrate-tick life cycle, in which the principal tick vectors Rhipicephalus and Haemaphysalis species, localize its distribution in ruminant populations to East Africa and South Asia (where the virus is known as the Ganjam virus), respectively ( ). Few serological assays have been developed to allow the analysis of antibody dynamics over the course of infections as well as the detection of previous exposures to bunyaviruses including Rift valley fever virus (RVFV), CCHFV, Cache valley virus, Akabane virus, Schmallenberg virus and NSDV ( ). Of note, NSDV-specific antibodies remain detectable in sheep for over a year post infection ( ); hence testing small ruminants offers a possible method to survey NSDV circulation. The format of such serological assays includes virus neutralization tests, indirect immunofluorescence assays and Enzyme Linked Immunosorbent Assays (ELISAs) using virus preparation or nucleoprotein (NP) as bait ( ). Recently, work by Belij-Rammerstorfer et al. ( ) has utilized the Glycoprotein C (Gc) as a test antigen in an in-house ELISA; developed as a sensitive and specific alternative to NP-based ELISAs for assessing CCHFV circulation in small ruminants. A disadvantage of serological assays lies with cross-reactivity. It happens when serum antibodies react to antigens from a virus the animal has not been exposed to, which may cause false positive misclassification of tested animals. Such cross-reactivities have been reported for members of the Orthonairovirus genus in the late 1970s and the early 1980s by means of immunofluorescence, haemagglutination inhibition and virus neutralization tests, using a combination of mouse ascetic fluids raised against a few orthonairoviruses and their corresponding antigens ( , ). More recently, cross-reactivity has been demonstrated experimentally between related orthonairoviruses with overlapping distributions, including CCHFV, NSDV and Dugbe virus (DUGV); with the latter circulating in ruminant populations in Africa including Uganda ( ), Ghana ( ), Kenya ( ), South Africa ( ) without eliciting a symptomatic infection in this host species ( , ). In fact, Hartlaub et al. observed that serum antibodies from a sheep immunized against DUGV, binds to cells expressing CCHFV glycoprotein precursor (CCHFV GPC), by employing a commercial indirect immunofluorescent assay; and to CCHFV NP by western blot ( ). Moreover, sera raised against NSDV and DUGV from experimentally infected and immunized ruminants displayed cross-neutralizations when assayed for their ability to neutralize each virus by 80% plaque reduction neutralization tests (PRNT 80 ), hence reducing the analytical specificity of these assays and possibly causing false-positive misclassification ( ). Advancing on such experimental findings, cross-reactivity has been investigated using bovine field sera from a region of CCHFV and DUGV co-circulation ( ). While no correlation was identified between CCHFV- and DUGV-specific antibody responses for respective in-house NP-based ELISAs, the commercial CCHFV Gc-based immunofluorescence assay was highly cross-reactive. However, since CCHFV and DUGV co-circulate in the region from that study, the possibility of a co-infection could not be excluded.

To investigate the effect cross-reactivity has on commonly used field serological assays, we used the understudied CCHFV and NSDV cross-reaction as a model, focusing on a sample set from a region where CCHFV, but neither NSDV nor DUGV are circulating. In this set-up, any CCHFV seropositive animals that tested positive for NSDV would be the result of cross-reactivity. Since NSDV has never been reported in Europe, a large set of sheep sera from Bulgaria, collected as part of a serosurvey in 2017, and previously screened against CCHFV NP and Gc antigens ( ), were tested against in-house NSDV NP-specific and Gc-specific IgG ELISAs. The possible cross-reaction was also tested on an in-house PRNT 80 assay, allowing us to assess whether CCHFV-endemic field sera can cross-neutralize NSDV in vitro . In addition to this, a small subset of sera from sheep experimentally infected with NSDV were tested with CCHFV NP-specific and Gc-specific ELISAs, in this case, animal sera that react to CCHFV antigens would be the result of a cross-reaction. While a commercial CCHFV-specific serological test was employed as gold standard, we also utilized a formaldehyde-inactivated whole NSDV as antigen in ELISA to confirm seroconversion of NSDV-infected sheep. Finally, potential causes for the observed cross-reactivity were explored by means of protein deglycosylation and analysis of available sequences of epitopes targeted by serum antibodies. Materials and methods Viruses and cells NSDV isolate ND66 PC9 was used; initially obtained from Dr Piet van Rijn, Central Veterinary Institute of Wageningen, Netherlands ( ). NSDV was passaged three times on BHK21, with subsequent virus stocks used in both back-titration and neutralization tests. The virus was prepared as follows: BHK21 were seeded in 175cm 2 flasks and cultured until 90-100% of confluence, then they were washed in PBS and 15 ml of virus diluted 1:1000 in FBS- and antibiotic-free Glasgow minimum essential medium (GMEM, Cat # G5154, Sigma-Aldrich) was added onto cells. The inoculum was removed after an hour and cells were cultured in 45 ml of complete GMEM containing 2% FBS. Cells were kept for 3 days until cytopathic effects (CPE) appeared. The medium containing virus particles was harvested and clarified by centrifuged at 3500 × g for 10 minutes to remove cellular debris. BSR-T7 cells were cultured in complete DMEM made of Dulbecco’s modified eagle medium (DMEM, Cat # D5796, Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with 10% foetal bovine serum (FBS, Cat # 10270106, Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1% penicillin/streptomycin (P/S, Cat # P4333, Sigma-Aldrich). Cells were grown to confluency in T175 flasks by incubating at 37°C and 5% CO 2 . BSR-T7 cells were used in both plaque assay and PRNT 80 methods. Results Cross-reaction among CCHFV-endemic field sera CCHFV-endemic field sera (n=1198) previously tested against CCHFV NP and Gc ( ) were assayed against NSDV NP and Gc (this study; ). The distributions of OD value for all four antigens were not normally distributed (Jarque-Bera test, p < 0.05). Anti-CCHFV NP-specific and anti-NSDV Gc-specific were skewed to the right while CCHF-Gc specific exhibit a bimodal distribution ( ). Hence, Spearman’s correlation test was performed to assess whether a correlation exists between OD values from both assays, i.e. whether sera strongly reacting to CCHFV NP and Gc tend to strongly react to respective NSDV antigens. A strong Spearman’s correlation coefficient was obtained when CCHFV Gc values were tested against NSDV Gc (Rho = 0.810, p < 0.001). Moreover, two populations of animals whose sera were reactive to both NSDV and CCHFV Gc could be observed ( , right panel). Conversely, a smaller correlation coefficient was found when testing CCHFV NP against NSDV NP values (Rho = 0.270, p < 0.001). Notably, only a diffuse population could be observed with a shift towards high CCHFV OD values but not necessarily high NSDV OD values. In our previous study ( ), a cut-off value for positivity was estimated using a finite mixture model for both CCHFV NP (0.234) or Gc (0.225). Such cut-off values were similar to the average OD value plus two standard deviation (μ + 2δ) obtained for sheep sera taken from sheep in the UK where CCHFV is absent (for NP: 0.239; for Gc: 0.222). We reported 413 and 461 positives samples out of 1200 sera for CCHFV NP and Gc, respectively. Based on this observation, we have included a set of sheep sera from the UK (n = 180), that have been screened against NP and Gc for both NSDV and CCHFV ( , open circles). We have estimated a cut-off value for NSDV NP and Gc using the μ + 2δ formula applied to the 180 UK sheep sera herein. Cut-off values were 0.293 for NSDV NP and 0.139 for NSDV Gc. We then applied this cut-offs to estimate the amount of sera that classify as positive for NSDV NP and Gc within the 410 and 460 sera that were classified as positives for CCHFV NP and Gc, respectively. 235 sera were positive for NSDV NP out of 410 CCHFV NP positives (57.3%), while 439 sera were positive for NSDV Gc out of 460 CCHFV Gc positives (95.4%). Furthermore, to quantify the agreement between the assays (as a proxy for cross-reaction), Cohen’s Kappa test was employed following classification of positive/negative, to the CCHFV-endemic field sera (n=1198) and sheep sera from the UK (n = 180). Regarding CCHFV-endemic field samples, the test reported a fair agreement between CCHFV NP and NSDV NP assays (Kappa statistics = 0.209), while it reported a substantial agreement between CCHFV Gc and NSDV Gc (Kappa statistics = 0.681) (see ). Using the sheep sera from the UK, only one sample was classified as positive for CCHFV Gc and six for NSDV Gc, while none was positive for CCHFV NP and two for NSDV NP ( ). All OD values for responses to all NPs did not increase for the entire course of infection and remained below the set cut-off. For NSDV NP, most responses were above the estimated cut-off using UK negative sheep sera from 0 dpi. This suggestive of an absence of responses mounted in comparison to day 0. Regarding responses to Gn, antibody response from two animals towards NSDV Gn spiked at 11 dpi and were above the set cut-off (VU16 and VU18). To get more insight into these antibody responses, we have also analyzed the response of each animal during the course of infection as a fold-increase to the response measured at 0 dpi. The responses observed at 11 dpi were substantially higher than that at 0 dpi for NSDV Gc, NSDV Gn (2/3 animals) and CCHFV Gc, displaying more than a 5-fold increase ( ). Altogether, for all sheep sera available by 11 dpi, similar responses were measured towards NSDV Gc and CCHFV Gc. Since these sheep were only exposed to NSDV, our observation is suggestive of a particular cross-reaction of NSDV-seropositive individual towards CCHFV Gc. To get an insight into this, publications that studied anti-CCHFV NP and Gc antibody targets were identified from PubMed database. Fifteen articles determined regions and precise epitopes bound by antibodies from different species (mouse, human, sheep, goat, cattle – ). Only four studies mapped linear epitopes bound by serum from sheep with a history of CCHFV exposure (see , green highlights). For NP, it has been suggested that the central portion of the protein is immunodominant ( – ; ), and so the majority of antibodies are directed against that region. In this region, most epitopes identified using sheep sera present highly divergent motif sequences to CCHFV ( ). In addition, there are epitopes near the C-terminus, in a region of high similarity outside the immunodominant region of NP; these are potentially involved in the weak cross-reactivity displayed by NP. Regarding the Gc, there was only one study that assessed sheep serum antibody binding epitopes ( ). Of the 7 reported epitopes, only 2 were found in a portion of Gc that are relatively conserved (>70%; ; ). However, we could not find any study reporting the location of the immunodominant region(s) of Gc. Furthermore, all epitopes targeted by sheep antibodies that have been reported are linear. Two articles detail conformational epitopes in the Gc using human-derived monoclonal antibodies ( , ). When aligning amino acid sequences of CCHFV and NSDV Gc used in our study, half of the binding motifs of these monoclonal antibodies were identical (10/20 and 9/17, respectively). However, when testing mouse monoclonal antibodies known to bind conformational epitopes ( ), they did not react to NSDV Gc ( ). Altogether, presented data suggest that the NP is lowly cross-reactive due to dominant epitopes being highly dissimilar between CCHFV and NSDV. However, Gc cross-reactivity requires further investigation. Discussion Small ruminants act as hosts and ‘reservoirs’ for several Orthonairovirus genus member viruses and as such, are often the target of surveillance programmes which utilize serological assays to indicate the presence of circulating antibodies. Cross-reactivity between members of the Orthonairovirus genus has been demonstrated to reduce the specificity of virus-specific serological assays, both experimentally ( ) and in the field (in regions where more than one orthonairoviruses are circulating), leaving unclear if what is observed is cross-reaction or co-infection ( ). To advance such work, we focused on serum antibody responses to CCHFV and NSDV, employing field sheep sera from a region where CCHFV circulates ( ) but NSDV is evidently absent ( ), eliminating the potential effect of co-infection when studying cross-reactivity. To assess the cross-reactivity of NP and Gc antigens, in-house NP-specific and Gc-specific ELISAs as well as a PRNT 80 were developed for NSDV. First, a large subset of sheep field sera sampled from a region where CCHFV is endemic and NSDV is known to be absent was utilized; allowing the quantification of the effect cross-reactivity is having on these assays, by comparing previously tested anti-CCHFV responses ( ) with anti-NSDV responses. A significant positive correlation between anti-CCHFV and anti-NSDV Gc-specific responses of CCHFV-endemic field sera tested on our in-house Gc-specific ELISAs indicated a strong cross-reactivity of antibodies towards Gc. To confirm this observed cross-reaction in field sera, a second subset of sera that have been harvested during the course of a controlled NSDV inoculation in sheep, were tested against both NSDV and CCHFV Gc antigens on in-house ELISAs. Our results show NSDV infected sheep display a seroconversion of anti-NSDV Gc-specific antibodies across 11 days. Meanwhile and despite a low sample size, the presence of NSDV-specific antibodies able to react to the CCHFV Gc supported evidence of this cross-reaction that could be seen in field samples. Furthermore, Cohen’s Kappa test reported a substantial agreement (Kappa statistics = 0.769) for CCHFV Gc and NSDV Gc assays performed on these experimental samples ( ). These results validate previous evidence of orthonairovirus glycoprotein cross-reactivity, with DUGV seropositive samples previously testing positive on a commercial species-adapted immunofluorescence assay based on CCHFV glycoprotein-expressing cells ( ). In regions where two or more orthonairoviruses overlap in their distribution ranges, such findings suggest Gc-based ELISAs would be potentially ineffective in correctly identifying which Orthonairovirus genus member is circulating in small ruminant populations. Therefore, confirmation using a virus neutralization test such as PRNT 80 would be highly recommended in these settings. Despite being subject to cross-reactions, Gc-based ELISA remains a valuable tool for studying the nature of immune responses in domestic animals, notably when the nature of viruses circulating in the area is known or in a controlled experimental setup. To assess whether N-linked Glycosylation of the Gc was responsible for cross-reactivity observed in our previous experiments, a small subset of ‘high’ anti-NSDV responding sera were tested against Gc with its N-linked glycosylation removed. When compared to the naïve Gc control, no significant difference in OD value was observed. These results suggested that this glycosylation was not the cause of exhibited cross-reactivity and instead, a conserved epitope is responsible for such a cross-reaction with further research necessary to identify this. Nonetheless, it appears that NP is less cross-reactive due to its dominant epitopes being highly dissimilar between CCHFV and NSDV. NP-based assays, in particular NP-based ELISAs, have previously been demonstrated to have high specificity for individual orthonairoviruses when tested against highly related species experimentally ( ) and in the field ( ). However, to confidently estimate the effect such cross-reactivity is having in a field setting, without the effect of co-infection on our sample set, our large CCHFV-endemic field sera sample set was used to assess the CCHFV/NSDV cross-reaction model. A weakly positive correlation between anti-CCHFV and anti-NSDV NP-specific responses of CCHFV-endemic field sera was observed on our in-house NP-specific ELISAs. To confirm this evidence of a weak cross-reaction between NSDV and CCHFV NP, sera from sheep experimentally infected against NSDV were tested against CCHFV and NSDV NP on in-house ELISAs. No seroconversion of NSDV NP antibodies occurred over 11dpi and so as expected, no CCHFV NP responses were also identified. The lack of seroconversion of NSDV NP antibodies prior to 11dpi followed evidence from Hartlaub et al. ( ). The authors suggested a seroconversion of anti-NSDV NP-specific antibodies further into the NSDV infection timeline, with antibodies of high-dose inoculated sheep first detectable in all sheep 15dpi. Data presented here continues to support NP-based ELISAs as the most specific test antigen for field ELISAs in comparison to Gc-based ELISAs. However, there are indications that the dynamics (Gc-specific responses appeared earlier than NP, this study) and nature of antibody responses (there are proportions of animals that are seropositive for Gc but not NP, see 14) may differ based on the animals and antigen screened. Future experiments must be conducted over a longer infection period to effectively assess cross-reactions over the NP seroconversion timeline. DUGV and Hazara virus (HAZV) anti-sera have previously been reported to cross-neutralize NSDV infection, suggesting anti-orthonairovirus responses to be capable of cross-neutralizing infection of highly related Orthonairovirus genus members ( ). To see whether CCHFV anti-sera was capable of neutralizing NSDV in vitro , a subset of ‘high’ anti-CCHFV and anti-NSDV responding sera on our in-house NP- and Gc- based ELISAs were tested on an in-house PRNT 80 assay. Only marginal cross-neutralization of NSDV was observed, with only 1/224 CCHFV-endemic field samples testing positive on this test format. Neutralization tests are time consuming, require trained laboratory personnel and must be carried out in appropriate containment conditions (BSL2: NSDV, BSL4: CCHFV). In addition, previous reports of strong cross-neutralization between NSDV and highly related co-circulating Orthonairovirus genus members such as DUGV ( ) restricts this assay for use in regions where only NSDV is present in small ruminant populations. Conclusion In this report, we assessed the existence of a cross-reactivity of sheep serum antibodies towards CCHFV and NSDV antigens as well as assess cross-neutralization of CCHFV-endemic field sera against NSDV using an in-house neutralization test. While the Gc exhibited a strong cross-reaction, the NP was weakly cross-reactive, hence being the antigen recommended for serological assays to distinguish between CCHFV and NSDV in regions where both co-circulate. Conclusion In this report, we assessed the existence of a cross-reactivity of sheep serum antibodies towards CCHFV and NSDV antigens as well as assess cross-neutralization of CCHFV-endemic field sera against NSDV using an in-house neutralization test. While the Gc exhibited a strong cross-reaction, the NP was weakly cross-reactive, hence being the antigen recommended for serological assays to distinguish between CCHFV and NSDV in regions where both co-circulate. The lack of cross-neutralization using our in-house PRNT 80 suggested positive samples were indeed cross-reactive and not co-infected. Due to limitations with required laboratory conditions, we suggest this assay could be used as a confirmatory test following initial screening using ELISA tests in areas where many Orthonairovirus are circulating. Finally, while few studies have unravelled the amino acid sequence of the immunodominant region of NP targeted by serum antibodies, the same should be carried out for Gc, potentially revealing epitopes responsible for this cross-reaction. This may allow the design of a recombinant antigen capable of mitigating this phenomenon.

Research insights What is currently known about this topic? Type 2 diabetes shows clinical heterogeneity which cannot be fully captured by glycemic metrics. Previous studies have attempted to identify diabetes subtypes through data-driven methods such as k-means. A novel method capturing the spatial phenotypes of diabetes enables a more comprehensive assessment of progression risks than clustering models. What is the key research question? Can routine clinical biomarkers identify distinct risk trajectories in type 2 diabetes and thereby inform targeted lifestyle or mechanism-based management strategies? What is new? Continuous disease mapping revealed spatially distinct distributions of clinical features and disease risks, with subgroups exhibiting differential proteomic signatures and varied sensitivity to lifestyle factors. How might this study influence clinical practice? Integrating deep phenotyping, proteomic profiling, and lifestyle interaction provides a framework for precision diabetes medicine, with potential to improve risk stratification and tailor personalized preventive strategies. Introduction Diabetes represents a significant global health concern, affecting an estimated one out of every nine adults worldwide [ , ]. The disease exhibits considerable heterogeneity in pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and risk of complications, complicating patient management and treatment efficacy [ ]. Elucidating this heterogeneity is therefore essential for advancing toward personalized care and improving long-term outcomes. Clustering approaches, such as k-means, have been widely used to delineate heterogeneity in type 2 diabetes by categorizing patients into discrete subgroups based on clinical variables. While these methods have helped reveal differential risks of progression and complications across subgroups, they possess inherent limitations [ – ]. These hard-clustering approaches do not provide individualized risk predictions, and fail to capture the continuous nature of disease progression, potentially oversimplifying the complex physiological spectrum of diabetes [ ]. The discriminative dimensionality reduction with trees (DDRTree) algorithm enables the generation of a branched tree structure that provides an intuitive visualization of the diabetes phenotypic spectrum [ ]. However, the application of this continuous modeling approach to systematically map a broad spectrum of diabetes-associated diseases and to link this phenotypic architecture to both lifestyle factors and proteomic signatures remains limited. Whether such a framework can provide insights into heterogeneous disease mechanisms and inform personalized management strategies is still largely unexplored. Therefore, in this study we applied the DDRTree method to model the continuous heterogeneity of type 2 diabetes across two independent cohorts—the UK Biobank and the Dongfeng-Tongji Diabetes Cohort (DFTJDC). We systematically examined diabetes-associated disease distributions across the phenotypic spectrum and assessed phenotype-specific associations with lifestyle factors. Finally, we sought to elucidate pattern-specific pathogenic mechanisms and identify potential molecular targets through proteomic profiling. Methods Study design and participants The UK Biobank is a large-scale, prospective study that involved over 500,000 participants aged 37–73 years from 22 centers across the United Kingdom between 2006 and 2010. The DFTJDC is an ongoing prospective study initiated in 2018 in Shiyan, Hubei Province, China, designed to investigate risk factors, complications, and prognosis of diabetes. Diagnostic criteria for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes are detailed in Supplementary Methods. Participants with diabetes before age 35 (likely type 1 diabetes), those with incomplete data on clinical risk factors and those with the outlier values (exceeding 5 standard deviation [SD] from the mean of the clinical measures) were excluded, leaving 6406 and 828 participants from UKB and DFTJDC, respectively. Assessment of diabetes-associated diseases Data on incident diseases were identified through electronic health records including those from hospital admissions, primary care, and death registers. In UKB, electronic health records were available up to 1 March 2022, 12 November 2021, and 25 October 2021 for centers in England, Wales, and Scotland, respectively. In DFTJDC, the electronic health records were available up to 26 November 2024. We considered macrovascular and microvascular complications, cancer, neurological and mental diseases, respiratory system disorders in both cohorts. Disease outcomes were identified using the International Classification of Diseases, 10th version (ICD-10) code (Supplementary Table ). Measurements of type 2 diabetes-related phenotypic variables We included seven routinely recorded phenotypic characteristics relevant to type 2 diabetes pathophysiology and associated with variation in risks of adverse outcomes: body mass index (BMI), high density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), triglyceride (TG), HbA1c, systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and total cholesterol (TC). These variables were selected a priori based on a previously established DDRTree-based phenotypic framework [ ]. In addition, five other clinical variables were also considered: waist hip ratio (WHR), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), c-reactive protein (CRP), and creatinine. Proteomic profiling The UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP) profiled 2923 plasma proteins using Olink’s proximity extension assay for 46,788 randomly selected participants, a representative subset of the full cohort. Details of data processing and quality control are available in Sun et al. [ ] study. Briefly, plasma samples were stored at − 80 °C before being analyzed in Sweden. Protein expression was quantified as normalized protein expression (NPX) values on a log2-transformed scale. After excluding eight proteins with missing values exceeding 20%, 2915 proteins were retained and standardized for subsequent analyses. Ultimately, proteomic analyses were conducted among 557 participants who were randomly selected by the UKB-PPP. Statistical analysis Baseline characteristics of the study participants were presented as mean ± SD for continuous variables, and as number (percentage) for categorical variables. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.4.1). In the following sections, a branch refers to a spatial segment of the tree structure inferred by DDRTree. A phenotype denotes to the set of clinical characteristics associated with each branch, summarizing the overall clinical profile of individuals located along that branch. Building on this framework, a pattern represents a higher-level integration of multiple phenotypes that exhibit similar disease-risk distributions, thereby grouping phenotypes according to common profiles of disease susceptibility. DDRTree DDRTree is a dimensionality reduction algorithm that projects multi-dimensional phenotypic data into a two-dimensional tree, revealing a spectrum form mixed phenotypes in the central trunk to distinct profiles in the branches [ , ]. For the UKB analyses, we applied DDRTree using the Monocle package (version 2.34.0) to seven quantitative variables [ ]. These variables were first standardized using a rank-based inverse normal transformation and then residualized for age and sex via linear regression. The resulting matrix was used to construct the final two-dimensional tree. Internal validation The UKB cohort was randomly divided into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets with comparable baseline characteristics (Supplementary Table ). In the training set, phenotypic variables were reduced to two dimensions (Dim1 and Dim2) using the DDRTree algorithm. Then a generalized additive model (GAM) incorporating age, sex and seven variables was fitted to predict these dimensions. Model performance was evaluated in the testing set by comparing predicted values with DDRTree-derived coordinates using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients (ρ). To further evaluate stability, we calculated the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) across 100 subsampling iterations, each excluding 10% of participants and remodeling the DDRTree. Consistency of branch assignments was quantified by pairwise ARIs, with ARI > 0.65 considered evidence of good stability (see Supplementary Methods). Risk estimation of diabetes-associated diseases To assess the 5-year and 10-year individual risk for each type 2 diabetes-associated diseases, we calculated predicted probabilities from competing risk models (Fine-Gray models) using tree dimensions 1 and 2 (Dim1 and Dim2) as independent variables. All-cause mortality was treated as a competing event. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated per one-unit increase in each dimension. To mitigate reverse causation, we excluded individuals who developed outcomes within the first year of follow-up. Quantitative the distribution pattern across the tree Beyond the visual gradient, we assessed the spatial distribution of phenotypic profiles and outcomes using two metrics. First, phenotypic distributions were regressed against the two tree dimensions, and outcome probabilities were estimated with competing risk models to depict risk gradient. Second, global and local Moran’s I statistics quantified spatial autocorrelation, with local Moran’s I based on 100 nearest neighbors. Detailed information is provided in the Supplementary Methods. We develop an interactive R shiny app that positions newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes patients within the phenotypic tree structure using mapping function. The application employs Cox models incorporating age, sex, and seven clinical variables to estimate complication risks, with model performance quantified by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results Phenotypic characteristics description and model performance Phenotypic characteristics of UKB and DFTJDC are described in Supplementary Tables and . Participants in the UKB had a mean age of 59.10 (SD = 7.17) years, 39.4% were female. Participants in the DFTJDC had a mean age of 56.3 (SD = 12.06) years, 35.0% were female. The seven variables used to construct the tree in the UKB, along with their mean (SD) values, were as follows: BMI (31.67 [5.70] kg/m 2 ), HDL-C (1.19 [0.30] mmol/L), TG (2.35 [1.30] mmol/L), TC (5.01 [1.27] mmol/L), HbA1c (53.90 [14.65] mmol/mol), SBP (143.31 [17.49] mmHg), and DBP (84.39 [9.92] mmHg). In the UKB, the GAM models predicting the two DDRTree dimensions demonstrated strong performance (adjusted R 2 values of 0.87 for Dim1 and 0.83 for Dim2; Supplementary Table ) and high concordance between predicted and actual dimension values (ρ Dim1 = 0.98, ρ Dim2 = 0.96). Internal validation yielded a median ARI of 0.87 (IQR 0.79–0.94), indicating robust model stability (Supplementary Fig. ). Phenotypic heterogeneity at type 2 diabetes diagnosis in UKB Phenotypic heterogeneity was systematically mapped onto the tree, revealing distinct spatial distributions for seven clinical variables (Fig. A). Two complementary metrics quantified these patterns. First, regression analyses demonstrated significant gradients along both tree dimensions (Fig. B and Supplementary Table ). BMI and TG were enriched in the upper-left branches and reversely related to HDL-C, which localized to the lower-right region. Blood pressure (SBP and DBP) increased toward the upper-right branches, whereas HbA1c and TC decreased along dimension 1 and dimension 2, respectively. Second, spatial autocorrelation confirmed significant clustering: global Moran’s I -values indicated that HDL-C and blood pressure exhibited the strongest spatial structure, followed by TG, BMI, TC, and HbA1c (Fig. C), with local patterns detailed in Supplementary Fig. . Additional variables, including WHR, ALT, AST, creatinine, and CRP, conformed to the BMI and TG gradient, while gamma-glutamyl transferase paralleled the distribution of HbA1c (Supplementary Tables and Supplementary Fig. ). Based on these distributions, five phenotypes were identified from the distal branches of the tree, excluding the central region with mixed features (Fig. D, Supplementary Tables and , Supplementary Fig. ). Phenotype 1 was characterized by concurrent elevations in adiposity, TG, HbA1c, blood pressure, liver enzymes, creatinine, and CRP, coupled with low HDL-C and TC. Phenotype 3 exhibited the opposite profile, with high TC, HDL-C, and blood pressure, but low adiposity, TG, and inflammatory/hepatic markers. Phenotype 2 was defined primarily by elevated blood pressure. Phenotype 4 and 5 shared increased HbA1c and TC with normal blood pressure; however, phenotype 4 displayed high HDL-C, whereas phenotype 5 was distinguished by obesity and elevated TG. Heterogeneity of diabetes-associated diseases in UKB During a median follow-up of 12.6 years, incident cases ranged from 224 to 1613 for macrovascular diseases, 242 to 793 for microvascular diseases, 1365 for cancer, 64 to 513 for neurological and mental diseases, 416 for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and 360 for non-alcohol fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Five-year progression probabilities and corresponding HRs from competing risk models were mapped across the tree (Fig. A, B). Significant global and local spatial autocorrelation was observed for all outcomes (Fig. C and Supplementary Fig. ). Three distinct spatial disease patterns were identified. The first pattern, located in the upper-left branches (phenotype 1 and 2), showed the highest risks for macrovascular diseases (excluding myocardial infarction [MI]), diabetic kidney disease (DK), Parkinson’s disease and NAFLD (HRs ranging from 0.67 to 0.91 for dimension 1; 1.27–1.55 for dimension 2). This cluster was characterized by higher adiposity, blood pressure, liver enzyme levels, and dyslipidemia (elevated TG and reduced HDL-C). The second pattern, localized to the left branches (phenotype 1, 4 and 5), was associated with increased risks of MI, diabetic neuropathy (DN), diabetic retinopathy (DR), depression and COPD. The third pattern, in the lower branches (phenotype 3–5), was linked to the highest risks of cancer and Alzheimer’s disease. This area was characterized by higher TC and HDL-C, although the associations with dimension 2 were borderline significant (Alzheimer, HR = 0.49, 95% CI = 0.23–1.02; cancer, HR = 0.93, 95% CI = 0.80–1.07). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these patterns. Adjustments for lifestyle factors (physical activity, sleep duration, smoking status, alcohol drinking status, and education levels) and baseline medication use (metformin, insulin, antihypertension, and lipid-lowering medication) did not materially alter these findings (Supplementary Table ), and the spatial associations remained consistent when assessed for 10-year disease progression probabilities (Supplementary Fig. ). Clustering analyses We performed phenotype classification using the K-means clustering method for comparative purpose. According to the Gap statistic, the Silhouette score, and the Elbow method, the optimal model was composed of two clusters (Supplementary Fig. ). Notably, cluster 1 exhibited adverse profiles across all phenotypic variables (BMI, TG, TC, HbA1c, SBP, DBP), but was not associated with elevated complication risk (Supplementary Table ). Mapping the k-means clusters onto the DDRTree structure revealed that both clusters aligned with five distinct phenotypes (Supplementary Fig. ). Differential associations of lifestyle factors with disease risks across type 2 diabetes phenotypes Given the number of incident cases available after stratification, we focused specifically on macrovascular and microvascular diseases (Table , Supplementary Table ). Overall, higher healthy lifestyle scores were consistently associated with reduced disease risk across all phenotypes, with HRs ranging from 0.80 to 0.88. However, the protective effects of specific lifestyle factors varied by phenotype. In phenotype 1, significant risk reduction was associated with regular physical activity (HR = 0.48), healthy sleep duration (HRs range = 0.64–0.74) and healthy diet (HRs range = 0.70–0.73), whereas alcohol consumption increased risk (HR = 1.70). For phenotype 2 and 5, healthy sleep duration (HRs range = 0.75–0.78) and nonsmoking (HRs range = 0.60–0.78) showed stronger protective effects, though alcohol consumption remained adverse in phenotype 5 (HR = 1.82). In contrast, regular physical activity (HRs range = 0.63–0.76) and nonsmoking (HRs range = 0.71–0.74) were the most salient protective factors in phenotype 3 and 4. Proteomic profile for type 2 diabetes phenotypes To elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms linking type 2 diabetes phenotypes to associated disease risks, we characterized their plasma proteomic profiles. Guided by the abovementioned disease distribution patterns, corresponding high- and low-risk subgroups were compared, identifying 44 and 50 differential proteins in the phenotype 1–2 vs. phenotype 3–5 and phenotype 1/4/5 vs. phenotype 2–3 comparisons, respectively (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.05/2,915; Supplementary Table ). KEGG and GO analysis revealed functional patterns across phenotypes (Supplementary Tables and , Supplementary Fig. ). Phenotype 1–2 were enriched in pathways related to metabolic imbalance and abnormal cardiac function, consistent with elevated risks of cardiovascular disease, DK, and NAFLD, and showed cytoskeleton and energy dysregulation linked to Parkinson’s disease. Phenotype 3–5 exhibited enrichment in immunity-inflammation activation, aberrant metabolism of chemical carcinogens, and drug resistance pathways, while phenotype 1/4/5 was characterized by chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, and lipid metabolic abnormalities. DDRTree analyses in DFTJDC Using the mapping function detailed in the Supplementary Methods, all participants from DFTJDC were mapped onto the CCDRFS tree, revealing distinct distributions for each phenotypic variable (Fig. ). Over a median follow-up of four years, we observed 74–145 macrovascular diseases, 110–115 microvascular diseases, 30 cancers, 40 COPD, and 175 NAFLD cases. The corresponding 5-year progression probabilities showed substantial variation across five phenotypes (Supplementary Fig. ). PAD and NAFLD risks were primarily driven by the combination of adiposity, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia and hypertension (clustered in phenotype 1–2), and cancer risk was concentrated in phenotype 4–5 with elevated TC and HDL-C; both patterns were consistent with those observed in UKB. In contrast, CVD, stroke, DK, and COPD risks clustered in phenotype 2–3 characterized by high blood pressure, adiposity, and hyperglycemia, and DR risk localized to phenotype 3–4 with higher blood pressure, TC and HDL-C, showing some divergence from UKB patterns. Visualizing individual risk in relation to their phenotype To support clinicians and patients in visualizing the risks of associated diseases in individuals with type 2 diabetes, we developed web applications ( https://dynamic-omics.shinyapps.io/ukb_shiny/ for UKB and https://dynamic-omics.shinyapps.io/dftjdc_shiny/ for DFTJDC). Each individual can be positioned within the phenotypic tree according to their risk profiles, allowing five-year predictions for macrovascular and microvascular diseases, cancer, neurological and mental diseases, and respiratory system disorders. Risk prediction models incorporated age, sex, and seven clinical variables defining the tree structure. In the UKB, using continuous phenotypic variables, along with age and sex, achieved AUCs of 0.58 to 0.83 for predicting diabetes-associated diseases. Incorporation of DDRTree dimensions resulted in slightly improved performance, with AUCs of 0.60 to 0.86. The highest discrimination was observed for Parkinson’s disease (AUC = 0.86), Alzheimer’s disease (0.83), DR (0.75), PAD (0.72), and DK (0.71). Internal validation in the UKB yielded AUCs of 0.51 to 0.84 in UKB, indicating good calibration. In the DFTJDC, models incorporating DDRTree dimensions achieved AUCs ranging from 0.58 to 0.75, with relatively better performance for stroke (AUC = 0.75), COPD (0.72), and CVD (0.72). Discussion Using seven routine clinical variables, we mapped the heterogeneity of type 2 diabetes across two independent populations through DDRTree. The resulting phenotypic structure, visualized as a branching tree, revealed a continuous spectrum of clinical profiles associated with distinct patterns of diabetes-associated diseases development and differential responses to lifestyle components. Proteomic signatures were identified as a key molecular correlate of these variations, representing one component of the broader biological processes underlying clinical heterogeneity. By integrating deep phenotyping, proteomic profiling, and lifestyle interaction analyses, this framework provides a foundation for precision medicine in type 2 diabetes, enabling improved risk stratification and tailored preventive strategies. Through the application of data-driven dimensionality reduction methodologies, clinical phenotypes within the UKB population manifested substantial gradients and joint distributions that were mapped in a “tree” structure: BMI and TG were enriched in the upper-left region, HbA1c was skewed toward the left, blood pressure (SBP/DBP) was concentrated in the upper-right, while HDL-C and TC were located in the lower-right and bottom sections, respectively. Diabetes-associated disease risks exhibited significant spatial clustering within specific regions of the tree, reinforcing the specific associations between phenotypic distribution and clinical outcomes. In the UKB, cardiovascular events and DK converged in the upper-left branch, representing an obesity-dominated metabolic syndrome phenotype. The co-distribution of clinical features within this phenotype is consistent with prior studies [ , ], and its associated clinical characteristics and complication risk profile resemble those reported by Asplund et al. [ ]. This region also exhibited increased risks of Parkinson’s disease and NAFLD, accompanied by elevated liver enzymes and creatinine levels—biomarkers of hepatic and renal dysfunction—suggesting coexisting metabolic abnormalities and shared pathogenic mechanisms. Proteomic profiling provides crucial molecular insights into the heterogeneity of diabetes. This molecular profile clearly explains their susceptibility to conventional cardiometabolic complications: disorders in lipid and energy metabolism directly drive atherosclerosis and hepatic steatosis [ , ], while abnormalities in cardiac structure and extracellular matrix remodeling form the pathological basis of heart failure and diabetic nephropathy [ ]. Notably, enrichment of inflammatory signaling, including cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction pathways, mirrors molecular features previously observed in insulin resistance–dominant diabetes subgroups, supporting the presence of shared inflammatory mechanisms underlying cardiometabolic vulnerability [ ]. In addition, aberrant expression of cytoskeletal and energy metabolism–related proteins may offer a molecular explanation for the elevated Parkinson’s disease risk observed in this region, suggesting a potential link between metabolic dysregulation and neurodegeneration [ ]. The risks of cancer and Alzheimer’s disease were significantly elevated in regions characterized by high TC and HDL-C, exhibiting a distribution pattern almost opposite to that of cardiovascular disease. This phenomenon may reveal an underlying pathophysiological “trade-off” between different disease categories [ ]. Although high HDL-C levels confer clear cardiovascular protection via reverse cholesterol transport, the concomitant persistent low-grade immune-inflammatory activation and aberrant DNA damage repair pathways in this phenotype may collectively create a common ground for both malignancies and neurodegeneration. Inflammatory mediators may promote tumor microenvironment formation and blood-brain barrier disruption in both peripheral and central nervous systems, while impaired DNA repair mechanisms further increase the risk of malignant transformation [ , ]. In other words, individuals with this phenotype may exist in a state of “relative metabolic health but immune dysregulation”, which protects them from conventional cardiometabolic diseases yet predisposes them to age-related conditions. Meanwhile, a phenotypic region primarily driven by severe hyperglycemia, accompanied by dyslipidemia and obesity, was strongly associated with the risks of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, retinopathy, depression, and COPD [ , ]. Proteomic analyses demonstrate consistent patterns of immune imbalance, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and enhanced apoptotic signaling across this subgroup. This shared pathophysiological mechanism systematically explains the co-aggregation of seemingly unrelated conditions. Specifically, the chronic inflammatory state may mediate microvascular complications through endothelial injury, contribute to depression and neuropathy by disrupting neurotransmitter balance and neuronal survival [ , ], and promote the tissue destruction and aberrant remodeling characteristic of COPD [ ]. To explore ethnicity-specific outcome associations, we projected data from a Chinese diabetic cohort into the DDRTree model previously established by Qiu et al. based on a Chinese population [ ]. The distribution patterns of core metabolic phenotypes-such as obesity, glycemia, and blood pressure—were well preserved in this cohort, strongly supporting the robustness of the type 2 diabetes heterogeneity framework in the Chinese population. We also observed cross-population consistency in diabetes-associated disease risks: for instance, the association between the obesity-dominant phenotype and cardiovascular disease, diabetic ketoacidosis, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease was consistently identified in both Chinese and UK cohorts. Notably, key ethnic differences emerged. In the Chinese population, the risk of diabetic retinopathy demonstrated a stronger association with hypertension, whereas in the UK population, retinopathy risk was more closely linked to hyperglycemia. These discrepancies may be attributed to a combination of genetic background, dietary habits-such as the influence of a traditional high-sodium diet on blood pressure in Chinese individuals-and differences in clinical practice [ ]. Together with the findings from Jia et al., which also emphasized the distinctive role of blood pressure phenotypes and their complication associations in Chinese individuals with diabetes, our results underscore the necessity of accounting for population-specific risk factor profiles when formulating precision prevention strategies. Our analysis goes beyond general “healthy living” advice, revealing distinct lifestyle-phenotype associations that may inform subtype-specific prevention strategies. Individuals in the upper-left DDRTree branch-characterized by high macrovascular and microvascular complication risk-significantly benefit from adequate physical activity, healthy sleep, and a healthy diet. Interestingly, non-smoking status did not demonstrate a significant independent protective effect within this phenotype, likely because obesity-driven cardiovascular risks outweigh the effects of smoking, and smoking-related weight loss may partially mask its hazards [ ]. Furthermore, in this metabolically dysregulated population, moderate alcohol intake did not show a protective effect against retinopathy compared with heavy intake, indicating that reducing or abstaining from alcohol is a more prudent recommendation. For the phenotype characterized mainly by hypertension (Cluster 2), the focus of clinical intervention should be on smoking cessation and maintaining healthy sleep duration. Both smoking and insufficient sleep are established strong risk factors that exacerbate blood pressure fluctuations and endothelial dysfunction [ ]. Interventions for this phenotype should integrate smoking cessation counseling and sleep hygiene management as components equally important to pharmacological blood pressure control. In the relatively metabolically healthy (Cluster 3) and high-TC (Cluster 4) phenotypes, regular physical activity is central to cardiovascular protection. Exercise enhances insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism—particularly through reverse cholesterol transport—making it a cornerstone non-pharmacological strategy [ ]. Among individuals with poor glycemic control (Cluster 5), not smoking and getting sufficient sleep are essential for reducing cardiovascular risk, likely through attenuating inflammation and autonomic dysfunction [ , ]. Additionally, alcohol abstinence is critical in this group to protect against microvascular complications such as retinopathy. Our study has several strengths. First, the DDRTree dimensionality reduction and visualization method provides a continuous representation of diabetes heterogeneity by mapping individuals onto a disease spectrum, thereby offering more information than hard clustering algorithms. Furthermore, our work integrates phenotypic distribution, complication risks, responsiveness to lifestyle factors, and proteomic mechanisms, yielding a systematic perspective on diabetes heterogeneity. Finally, the web-based tool we developed uses seven readily available clinical variables to deliver precise individual positioning within the phenotypic structure, offering practical potential for clinical guidance. We acknowledge that several limitations of our study should be considered. First, by excluding individuals with long-standing diabetes, our findings may not fully represent the broad spectrum of patients encountered in real-world clinical practice. Second, the observed subtype-specific lifestyle associations, while hypothesis-generating, are exploratory and require prospective validation in dedicated intervention trials.

Second, the observed subtype-specific lifestyle associations, while hypothesis-generating, are exploratory and require prospective validation in dedicated intervention trials. Third, the phenotypic structure was constructed using routinely available clinical variables, without inclusion of direct measures of insulin resistance or beta-cell function, which may limit the resolution of specific pathophysiological mechanisms underlying certain subtypes. Finally, due to sample size constraints, the Chinese cohort was projected onto the pre-existing DDRTree. Nevertheless, the consistent distribution patterns and outcome heterogeneity observed support the utility of this approach in populations of shared ethnicity. It is anticipated that future studies, incorporating diverse cohorts and multi-omics data, will facilitate a more refined understanding of the mechanisms underlying diabetic heterogeneity. Conclusions Using seven clinical variables, this study identified distinct phenotypes of type 2 diabetes, and further elucidated their differential risks for multiple complications via DDRTree. We further uncovered phenotype-specific associations with lifestyle factors and linked these clinical patterns to underlying proteomic mechanisms. Our work offers a systematic framework for understanding diabetes heterogeneity, and the intuitive visualization tool we developed shows potential to facilitate clinician-patient communication and shared decision-making in clinical practice. Background People Living With HIV/AIDS (PLWHA) have a higher risk of morbidity and mortality from acquiring infectious diseases, including those preventable by vaccination, and may experience prolonged disease progression, exacerbated symptoms, and increased hospitalization rates [ ]. Reducing severe infections is one of the most important measures to improve the quality and life expectancy of these people [ ]. Thus, immunization of PLWHA is imperative to reduce the incidence of vaccine-preventable diseases and improve their quality of life, being one of the most effective public health strategies for the prevention of infectious diseases and constituting a fundamental health intervention [ , ]. Among vaccine-preventable diseases, hepatitis caused by the hepatitis A and B viruses stands out. Hepatitis consists of inflammation of the liver that can be caused by several factors, including viral infection, the best known being A, B, C, D and E. Because it constitutes a challenge for health systems and the possibility of causing serious illnesses, the World Health Organization (WHO) has defined that by 2030 the incidence of new infections in the world should be reduced by 90%, reaching 520,000 cases per year [ ] (WHO, 2025). In Brazil, the Ministry of Health, aligned with WHO recommendations, proposes a series of strategies to municipalities aimed at eliminating viral hepatitis in the country, which includes diagnosing at least 90% of people with active infection and treating at least 80% of people with an indication for treatment [ , ]. Among PLWHA, hepatitis B is one of the main causes of hepatocellular carcinoma and mortality. Co-infection with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and hepatitis viruses can significantly influence the natural history of these infections, which impairs the prognosis of affected individuals, potentiates liver damage, and contributes to the accelerated progression of liver disease [ , ]. Regarding Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) infection, although acute HAV infection is self-limiting, infection in HIV-infected individuals can lead to a higher risk of mortality from chronic liver disease. Thus, it is recommended that susceptible HIV-positive individuals be vaccinated against HAV [ ]. Therefore, periodic screening for viral hepatitis among PLWHA is crucial for the early detection of these infectious agents, allowing for appropriate treatment and prevention of serious liver complications. In addition, they must have their vaccination status updated against HAV and Hepatitis B (HBV) from the time of HIV infection diagnosis [ ], contributing to global goals for the elimination of viral hepatitis. In Brazil, a downward trend in the incidence rates of HBV infection has been observed in recent years, reaching 4.7 cases/100,000 inhabitants in 2023, representing a 42.8% reduction since 2013. This progress is due to the introduction of the vaccine into the national vaccination schedule for children starting in 1998, with progressive release to the entire population [ , ]. According to data from the Ministry of Health, among the total number of reported cases of Hepatitis B from 2008 to 2023, 5.0% occurred in PLWHA [ ]. For hepatitis A, there is no data in Brazil regarding the number of cases in PLWHA. In the general population, however, the incidence showed slight variation between the years 2011 and 2014. From 2015 to 2022, a significant reduction of 74.3% in rates was observed, followed by an increase of 143.1% in 2023 [ ]. Improvements in people’s living conditions and health have contributed to the reduction in the circulation of HAV, thereby increasing the non-immune population, especially among younger people, which has contributed to the occurrence of outbreaks, mainly involving the category of unvaccinated Men Who Have Sex With Men (MSM) [ , ]. Because they share common transmission routes such as sexual transmission, HBV and HIV, and more recently have also become a significant route of transmission for hepatitis A due to oral-anal sexual practices or other forms of exposure to fecal matter, PLWHA, especially MSM, are considered a priority population for the prevention of viral hepatitis, presenting greater vulnerability to the acquisition of these viruses, which can be prevented through vaccination [ , , ]. The National Immunization Program (NIP) of the Brazilian Unified Health System (UHS) recommends in the vaccination schedule for adults living with HIV/AIDS the vaccines against hepatitis B and hepatitis A. For this, it is necessary to evaluate the vaccine doses received before the diagnosis of HIV infection and the immunity to these diseases to recommend vaccination [ ]. In this context, healthcare professionals, especially the nursing team plays a key role in administering vaccines and ensuring completion of the vaccination schedule for the various groups served at this functional site. To this end, they must be properly trained to assess the suitability and indication of each vaccination schedule according to the group and age group [ , ]. Furthermore, nurses conduct nursing consultations, during which they have the opportunity to guide individuals regarding the immunobiologicals recommended by the NIP and offered free of charge by the UHS. Little is known about the serological status and vaccination status of PLWHA in Brazil. Thus, this study aimed to analyze the immunity of men living with HIV to hepatitis A and B, with emphasis on those in the MSM category, to identify the factors associated with this immunity. Methods Design and setting of the study This is a retrospective analytical observational study using secondary data on cases of men living with HIV reported in the Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN), a Brazilian government national database used to register and monitor diseases and conditions subject to mandatory notification in the country. The municipality studied is located in the northeast of the state of São Paulo, Brazil, about 310 km from the capital, and has an estimated population of 728,400 inhabitants, being the 8th most populous municipality in the state compared to the other 645 municipalities [ ]. Population and sample The study population consisted of male PLWHA, aged 13 years or older, notified in SINAN between 2015 and 2020, residing in Ribeirão Preto/SP/Brazil, who were being followed up in the public network at municipal Specialized Care Services (SCS) with a diagnosis 180 days or less prior to the notification date in the system. Only individuals with adult HIV/AIDS notification in the SINAN, considered by the system to be 13 years or older, were included. We selected individuals diagnosed 180 days or less before diagnosis to obtain a more homogeneous sample, since notifications are not always made at the time of diagnosis and may be made years later. Patients who were registered with or receiving clinical follow-up in the supplementary health network and those receiving follow-up in the public health network other than the SCS, for which we did not have access to the information system, were excluded from the study. Individuals who relinquished their residency within the municipal boundaries, were transferred to follow-up in other municipalities, or perished during the study period were excluded from the analysis. Patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria were included in the study. Data collection The data was collected from a variety of Health Information Systems. Initially, the SINAN database was extracted with HIV cases reported in the system between 2015 and 2020. The utilisation of individuals’ identification data facilitated the aggregation of information from disparate information systems, given the absence of a unified national information system in Brazil. To facilitate data collection, a questionnaire was developed, evaluated by experts, and previously tested in a pilot study, which underwent modifications before the official data collection. The data collection process was conducted over the period from 2021 to 2022, utilising the aforementioned questionnaire. This questionnaire encompassed a range of sociodemographic and clinical variables, which were developed on the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap ® ) platform. Data regarding sex, skin color, date of birth, notification date, and diagnosis date were extracted from SINAN. Clinical information, test results, and vaccine doses received were extracted from the municipal information system (Hygia-RP System). To complement the unidentified data in the previous systems, the Laboratory Test Control System (SISCEL) was consulted for viral load and CD4 T cell count, and the National Immunization Program Information System in effect during the data collection period (SI-NIP Web) was consulted to evaluate registered vaccines when no record was found in the HYGIA-RP System. Variables of interest Immunity to hepatitis B was assessed using the result of the first anti-HBs serology (reactive/non-reactive) collected from the patient, and all results of this test available in the electronic medical record up to the date of the vaccination status assessment. Anti-HBs seropositivity, titers greater than or equal to 10 IU/mL, which confers protection against new infections, was the dependent variable in the hepatitis B analyses. In the first anti-HBs assessment, the first available test recorded in the system after the diagnosis of HIV infection was considered. Anti-HBs seropositivity, titers greater than or equal to 10 IU/mL, which confers protection against new infections, was the dependent variable in the hepatitis B analyses. In the first anti-HBs assessment, the first available test recorded in the system after the diagnosis of HIV infection was considered. Twenty-nine individuals were not included in the analysis because they did not have a result for this test in the system. For the assessment of vaccination status, the vaccines registered and the schedules indicated by the NIP at the time of the study were taken into consideration [ ]. For the hepatitis B vaccine, three doses were recommended for individuals who started vaccination before the HIV diagnosis. For those who started the vaccination schedule after the diagnosis, the recommended schedule was four doses, using twice the usual dose for the age group. This booster schedule was intended only for susceptible individuals who had not developed prior immunity through immunization or contact with the virus [ ]. In this study, considering the NIP regulations at the time of data collection, the hepatitis B vaccination schedule was considered adequate in the following situations: Individuals with a complete three-dose schedule performed before diagnosis; Those who received a four-dose schedule after diagnosis (with one or two schedules completed); Mixed schedule, initiated with three doses before diagnosis and completed in a four-dose schedule with a double dose; Two complete three-dose schedules; Combination of a three-dose schedule before and a four-dose schedule after diagnosis; Ongoing vaccination schedule, provided there are no delays. Individuals without indication for vaccination were excluded from the vaccination schedule analysis, including those with reactive anti-HBs without a record of vaccine doses and individuals with reactive HBsAg serology. Regarding the hepatitis A vaccine, available in the public network in special situations, which includes HIV infection, the recommended schedule was two doses with a six-month interval for non-immune individuals [ ]. Individuals with an adequate hepatitis A vaccination schedule were considered those who completed the indicated vaccination schedule with two doses or who had the schedule in progress without delays. Individuals with reactive anti-HAV IgG without a record of vaccine doses were not included in the vaccination schedule analysis. As variables related to social vulnerability, indicators that help identify groups or individuals at higher risk of exclusion were considered, such as chemical dependency (alcoholism, drug addiction), homelessness, and deprivation of liberty (detention). The other independent variables were skin color, age group, education level, health unit that performs clinical follow-up, MSM category, CD4 T-cell count, and adherence to Antiretroviral Therapy (ART), considered adherent in this study those individuals with medication withdrawal recorded in the system in the three months preceding the start of data collection. In regard to the TCD4 lymphocyte count, the results presented since HIV infection diagnosis until the point of data collection in SISCEL were evaluated, with particular attention paid to the lowest value documented. In accordance with the findings, the case was categorised within one of the following classifications: The presence of any count was categorised as follows: “presence of any count < 200”, “presence of any count between 200 and 350”, and “all counts > 300”. Data analysis After data collection was completed, the data were extracted from the REDCap ® platform into a Microsoft Office Excel ® spreadsheet and transferred to the IBM ® Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS ® ) program, version 25. A descriptive analysis was performed, where the data were presented in relative and absolute frequency. Fisher’s exact test was also performed to identify associations with the outcomes, adopting a significance level of 5%. Subsequently, a simple logistic regression of the outcomes with the variables that showed an association was performed. Finally, the independent variables with a p-value greater than or equal to 0.05 were included in the adjusted model. The data “not identified”/“exam not available”/“no information”/“not applicable”/“ignored”/“no indication” in the evaluated variables were treated as omitted during the analyses. Results 1971 HIV notifications from SINAN were analyzed, with electronic medical record evaluation of cases that met the study’s inclusion criteria.
